newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvians rap Fujimori's siege handling - poll.
newsitem.headline: Peruvians rap Fujimori's siege handling - poll.

text.p: Peruvians were growing strongly critical of President Alberto Fujimori's handling of the 110- day hostage crisis despite backing his pledges to find a negotiated solution, an opinion poll showed on Sunday.
The poll, published in the Lima newspaper El Comercio, showed approval for Fujimori's handling of the siege at the Japanese ambassador's house had plunged to 28 percent from 66 percent in January.

The poll, by consulting firm CPI in El Comercio, suggested impatience with the slow pace of talks to free the 72 hostages held by the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels. Twenty percent said the government should give more ground to win a solution and 49 percent said the MRTA should do so.

MRTA rebels stormed the house during a cocktail party on Dec. 17 and took some 500 guests hostage, later releasing all but a VIP list of 72 people including two cabinet ministers, Fujimori's brother and the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia.
Fujimori on Saturday renewed his pledge to find a negotiated settlement to the crisis, saying he would intervene with force only as a last resort in an "uncontrollable emergency."

With the siege dragging into its 16th week, Fujimori returned to Lima from Bolivia late on Saturday with words of support from his Bolivian counterpart Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada, and a vow to keep negotiating.

"We are not contemplating the use of force. The use of force is a move which would become the last (resort), useful in an uncontrollable emergency which we hope will not occur," Fujimori said in the Bolivian city of Santa Cruz.
"We will continue exhausting all efforts ... to reach a peaceful outcome," said Fujimori, admitting he had no idea when that might be.

A strong majority of Peruvians agree a negotiated solution should be sought. Eighty-one percent said Fujimori should shun force and use only negotiations to free the hostages, up from 76 percent in March.

But suggesting impatience for a deal to end the crisis, the number of respondents who called Fujimori's handling of the crisis only slightly ineffective or completely ineffective doubled to 62 percent from 34 percent in January.

Fujimori's overall approval rating was steady at 50 percent, unchanged from January, according to the poll of 400 people in Lima and the neighbouring city of Callao. The poll did not give a margin of error.
With talks reported to be languishing, speculation was rife in Lima that one of the crisis mediators had taken negotiations directly to the hostage-takers' leadership.

Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, a member of a three-man mediation team, visited a naval base in the port of Callao where the MRTA's maximum leader Victor Polay and at least two other MRTA prisoners are serving life sentences.

News reports said Cipriani spoke to Polay during the hour- long visit to the prison on Friday evening. Cipriani was silent about the visit, but early on Sunday, MRTA made a reference to the base in two new posters it hung from a residence window.

One poster said, "Down with the jail-tombs of the Callao naval base," and another saluted Polay on his 44th birthday on Sunday: "MRTA Commander Victor Polay, we salute you on your day. Your resistance and courage are an example for everyone."
Local newspapers speculated that Cipriani hoped Polay would persuade Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, leader of the MRTA guerrillas holed up in the diplomatic compound, to give up his struggle.
Fujimori's government has not met the hostage-takers for face-to-face talks since mid-March, leaving the mediation panel to carry out a kind of shuttle diplomacy between the two sides.
Fujimori was due to speak in a televised interview on Sunday night at 9 p.m. EST (0200 GMT).
Talks appear to have stalled on the issue of the MRTA's demands for freedom for about 450 jailed comrades in exchange for release of the hostages.
